{"sample_id": "blind-68baf8d474f84116b041f4cbc61e6aa4", "theorem": "I have an \(n \times n\) sheet of stamps, from which I've been asked to tear out blocks of three adjacent stamps in a single row or column. (I can only tear along the perforations separating adjacent stamps, and each block must come out of the sheet in one piece.) Let \(b(n)\) be the smallest number of blocks I can tear out and make it impossible to tear out any more blocks. Prove that there are real constants \(c\) and \(d\) such that

\[
\frac{1}{7} n^{2}-c n \leq b(n) \leq \frac{1}{5} n^{2}+d n
\]

for all \(n>0\).", "assumptions": [], "domain": "usamo", "explicit_subgoals": [], "candidate_text": "Take \(c=\frac27\) and \(d=8\). Here \(n\) is a positive integer.

For the lower bound, suppose \(n\ge3\), and consider any terminal configuration obtained after removing \(q\) disjoint blocks. Every original horizontal or vertical triple must meet a removed block; otherwise that triple could still be removed. There are
\[
2n(n-2)
\]
such triples.

A horizontal removed block meets at most five horizontal triples: their initial positions differ from that of the block by at most two. Each of its three cells lies in at most three vertical triples, so it meets at most nine vertical triples. Thus it meets at most \(14\) potential triples altogether. The same bound holds for a vertical block. Consequently
\[
14q\ge 2n(n-2),
\]
and hence every terminal configuration satisfies
\[
q\ge \frac17n^2-\frac27n.
\]
In particular this holds for \(q=b(n)\). For \(n=1,2\), we have \(b(n)=0\), and the same inequality remains valid.

For the upper bound, put \(m=\lfloor n/5\rfloor\) and \(N=5m\). In the \(N\times N\) subsquare, divide the cells into \(5\times5\) squares. In every such square remove the following five horizontal blocks, using local row and column coordinates:
\[
(1,1),(1,2),(1,3);\qquad (2,3),(2,4),(2,5);
\]
\[
(3,1),(3,2),(3,3);\qquad (4,3),(4,4),(4,5);
\]
\[
(5,2),(5,3),(5,4).
\]
These five blocks are disjoint.

The pattern repeats with period five. In rows of local type \(1,3\), the removed column residues are \(1,2,3\); in rows of type \(2,4\), they are \(3,4,5\); and in rows of type \(5\), they are \(2,3,4\). Thus no row contains three consecutive remaining cells, including across boundaries between adjacent \(5\times5\) squares.

In columns of local type \(1,2,3,4,5\), respectively, the removed row residues are
\[
\{1,3\},\quad \{1,3,5\},\quad \{1,2,3,4,5\},\quad \{2,4,5\},\quad \{2,4\}.
\]
Each periodically repeated set leaves runs of at most two consecutive cells. Hence no column of the \(N\times N\) subsquare contains three consecutive remaining cells.

There are \(m^2\) small squares, so this first stage uses \(5m^2=N^2/5\) blocks. Now greedily remove any further available block in the entire \(n\times n\) sheet until no block remains. Every block added at this stage contains a cell outside the \(N\times N\) subsquare, since that subsquare already contains no available triple. The added blocks are disjoint, so their number is at most
\[
n^2-N^2=(n-N)(n+N)\le 4(2n)=8n.
\]
Therefore the resulting terminal configuration uses at most
\[
5m^2+8n=\frac{N^2}{5}+8n\le \frac15n^2+8n
\]
blocks. By the definition of \(b(n)\),
\[
b(n)\le \frac15n^2+8n.
\]
Combining the two estimates gives, for every positive integer \(n\),
\[
\frac17n^2-\frac27n\le b(n)\le \frac15n^2+8n.
\]"}
